canonicalExplanation.summary: A component test can't tell you whether your **routes** are wired correctly: whether `/courses/python` really renders the Python page, whether links update the URL, or whether unknown paths show not-found. A **route integration test** renders the real route tree inside a `MemoryRouter` with `initialEntries` set to a starting URL, then clicks links like a learner and asserts **the URL, the heading, the title and where focus landed**. Include a test for an **unknown URL** and for **Back** navigation.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Every page component has passing tests, but after a refactor the "Python" link points to `/course/python` (missing an s) and learners land on not-found. No test caught it, because each page was tested alone. A test starts at /courses/c, activates Python, and asserts URL, heading, and focus context. In this lesson you'll create an integration test covering route navigation and focus-context changes.

```predict
{"question": "CoursePage has its own passing test. Does that prove the link from the C course to Python works?", "options": ["Yes", "No: only a test through the router checks the link's path and route config"], "answer": 1, "why": "Integration tests catch wiring mistakes between links and routes."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Accessibility, errors and performance** module, the **Routing and application context** module, **Asynchronous component tests**, and **Route titles and focus management**, since focus is part of what you'll assert.

sections.heading: The model: real routes, a starting URL, learner actions
What to cover

includes: Render the real route tree in a MemoryRouter at a starting URL.
Assert URL, heading, title and focus after navigation, plus not-found and Back.
excludes: End-to-end tests in a real browser.
Testing the hosting fallback (manual or deploy check).

outcomes: Create an integration test covering route navigation and focus-context changes.

examples.title: From the C course to the Python course
examples.situation: A test starts at /courses/c, activates Python, and asserts URL, heading, and focus context.
walkthrough: **Starts at /courses/c:** renderAt uses MemoryRouter with that initial entry and the real AppRoutes.
**Activates Python:** userEvent clicks the link found by its accessible name.
**Asserts URL, heading, and focus:** the test will check the path is /courses/python, the h1 says Python and has focus, and the title matches.
examples.result: The broken /course/python link fails this test immediately, and the fixed version proves the whole journey works.

examples.title: Back that went nowhere
examples.situation: After opening a lesson from a course, pressing Back in the app's own "Back to course" button does nothing, because it calls navigate(-1) on a directly opened URL with no history.
walkthrough: A direct visit has no previous entry to go back to.
Link to the course's real path instead of navigate(-1).
Test: renderAt the lesson URL directly, click "Back to course", and assert the course heading.
examples.result: The Back to course button works whether the learner came from the course or a shared link.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Testing the component alone proves route configuration and browser history behavior.
misconceptions.correction: A component test renders one page in isolation. Only rendering the real routes in a router, following links and checking the resulting URL and view proves the wiring and history behave.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "From the C course to the Python course", why did the page tests all pass?

analogy.example: Component tests check **each room of a house**; route tests check **the corridors and doors between them**. A perfect kitchen doesn't help if the door from the hall opens onto a wall.
usefulFor: MemoryRouter = a model house with a chosen front door
limitations: Houses don't have Back buttons; apps do, so test them.
An unknown address should lead to a clear sign, not a blank wall.

steps.explanation: The test starts at /courses/c with the real routes.
The test activates Python like a learner would.
It asserts URL, heading, and focus context after navigation.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a route integration test. Step 1, Start: location is /courses/c; heading is C. The test starts at /courses/c with the real routes. nearTransfer.prompt: Write a route test that starts at `/courses/css?page=abc` and asserts the list shows page 1, and one for `/courses/unknown` showing not-found.

farTransfer.prompt: Write an integration suite for your app's three main journeys: direct entry, link navigation with focus and title, Back navigation, invalid params and unknown URLs.
expectedEvidence: Suite passes and catches a deliberately broken link.
Focus and title asserted each time.

remediation.explanation: List the doors into each page: **direct URL, link, Back, bad params, unknown path.** Write a MemoryRouter test for each, asserting URL, heading, title and focus.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "Back that went nowhere".

recap.summary: To create an integration test covering route navigation and focus-context changes, render the real routes in a MemoryRouter at a starting URL, click links like a learner, assert the URL, heading, title and focused element, and add tests for Back, invalid parameters and unknown paths.
retrievalPrompts: Why don't component tests prove routing works?
Which four things should you assert after navigating?
